extracted.intended_audience: general polite reading public and aspiring essayists (tea-table audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short, informal periodical essays for a general polite audience (the 'tea-table'), emphasizing loose, conversational structure, moral instruction, tasteful humour, and appropriate use of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Looseness and freedom of an essay
rubrics_metrics.description: When I make Choice of a Subject that has not been treated on by others, I throw together my Reflections on it without any Order or Method, so that they may appear rather in the Looseness and Freedom of an Essay, than in the Regularity of a Set Discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer an informal, digressive voice for short essays: allow reflections to be thrown together rather than forced into a rigid, formal structure. Embrace conversational asides and a free ordering of thoughts to suit the essay form. Anti-pattern: forcing an essay into the 'regularity of a set discourse' which stifles the essay's natural freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose novel, untread subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: When I make Choice of a Subject that has not been treated on by others...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek subjects not already exhausted by others to keep the essay fresh and engaging. Originality of topic is valued. Example: pick everyday or domestic angles that others have overlooked. Scoring note: originality of subject contributes positively to the essay's appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: represent human nature to instruct
rubrics_metrics.description: Without presenting Vice under any false alluring Notions, [the papers] give my Reader an Insight into the Ways of Men, and represent human Nature in all its changeable Colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to portray the follies and varieties of human behaviour clearly so readers (especially the virtuous and innocent) can learn in speculation. Use realistic character sketches and examples that reveal 'ways of men' without glamorising vice. Anti-pattern: romanticizing or glamourizing immoral behaviour so as to allure rather than instruct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting vice as alluring
rubrics_metrics.description: Without presenting Vice under any false alluring Notions...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make immoral actions appear attractive or enviable. When depicting vice for satirical or instructive purposes, maintain a moral clarity that prevents corruption of susceptible readers. Example: satire should expose folly, not celebrate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open minds without vitiating them
rubrics_metrics.description: The Virtuous and the Innocent may know in Speculation what they could never arrive at by Practice, and by this Means avoid the Snares of the Crafty, the Corruptions of the Vicious, and the Reasonings of the Prejudiced. Their Minds may be opened without being vitiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write so that readers gain insight into worldly behaviours and dangers (speculation) but are not morally corrupted. Balance candid depiction with protective framing and clear moral lessons. Consider audience vulnerability when choosing examples and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject-matter to the tea-table audience
rubrics_metrics.description: As your Paper is Part of the Equipage of the Tea-Table, I conjure you to print what I now write to you... publish some which may tend to the Information of Mankind in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose pieces that suit domestic, social reading contexts (tea-table): accessible language, practical or conversational topics, and material of general information or instruction rather than highly technical or abstruse discourse. Anti-pattern: overly learned treatises that don't suit a general parlour readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone for oratory/vernacular speech: be tuned by good-nature, truth, discretion, sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: I would always have it tuned by Good-Nature, Truth, Discretion and Sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying speech (especially female oratory in the essay), prefer a tone characterized by kindness, honesty, discretion and sincerity. These virtues make speech pleasant and useful. Use this as positive criteria for dialogue, reported speech, and rhetorical passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disagreeable notes: anger, censoriousness, gossip, coquetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Cure it of several disagreeable Notes, and in particular of those little Jarrings and Dissonances which arise from Anger, Censoriousness, Gossiping and Coquetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of tones and devices that produce petty malice or mean-spiritedness: angry outbursts, gratuitous censorious remarks, idle gossip, or coquettish affectations. These are anti-patterns that harm the essay's moral and aesthetic effect. Revision check: remove or temper passages that veer into these registers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ridicule ethically – to correct vice, not to deride virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Talent of Ridicule were employed to laugh Men out of Vice and Folly, it might be of some Use to the World; but instead of this, we find that it is generally made use of to laugh Men out of Virtue and good Sense, by attacking every thing that is Solemn and Serious, Decent and Praiseworthy in Human Life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply satire and ridicule with an ethical aim: target folly and vice constructively rather than mocking what is serious and virtuous. Anti-pattern: defaulting to ridicule for mere entertainment that denigrates worthy sentiment or good sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of ridicule and appropriate register (comedy vs burlesque)
rubrics_metrics.description: The two great Branches of Ridicule in Writing are Comedy and Burlesque. The first ridicules Persons by drawing them in their proper Characters, the other by drawing them quite unlike themselves... where the low Character is to be raised, the Heroick is the proper Measure; but when an Hero is to be pulled down and degraded, it is done best in Doggerel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish technique: use comedy to expose characters by faithful representation; use burlesque to invert or contrast character with incongruous form. Choose metric/register to suit aim: heroic (grand verse) to elevate the low; doggerel to debase the grand. Practical guidance for satirical poets and dramatists on matching form to target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer anecdote and concrete example for moral persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The papers give my Reader an Insight into the Ways of Men, and represent human Nature in all its changeable Colours... I shall insert [letters and examples] ... because I think there is more Spirit and true Gallantry in it than in any Letter I have ever read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete anecdotes, letters, and short illustrative stories to make moral points vivid and persuasive. Anecdotes function as exempla that open the reader's understanding without abstract theorizing. Editorial note: include well-chosen, lively examples to enliven essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors that resonate (common, cross-cultural imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: The metaphor of Laughing, applied to Fields and Meadows when they are in Flower, or to Trees when they are in Blossom, runs through all Languages... This shews that we naturally regard Laughter, as what is in it self both amiable and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ metaphors with broad resonance — images that recur across cultures and languages — to tap shared sentiments and make scenes feel natural and beautiful. Avoid over-obscure or idiosyncratic conceits that will not land with a general audience.
